Spawned: full actor sharding and batching

1,575 measured processes, 1,575 successful; 129,024,105 validated requests. Five independent processes per cell. Existing public actor/protocol interfaces and production defaults are unchanged.

Variant suffixes -1/-16 mean message-turn size, not actor or thread count. All compared paths run actual Spawned actors, boxed envelopes, unbounded mailboxes, replies and lifecycle. This study replaces the previous native-loop semantic mismatch with a matched comparison. It does not erase runtime ownership, placement and compatibility differences.

Implementation and research questions · Validation and known test limitations · Raw data and hashes

Findings and recommendation

Keep Tokio as the default. Retain full-actor sharding as opt-in research for Linux workloads, with an explicit runtime owner and compatibility contract before considering a supported backend. The new matched comparison changes the earlier native-loop story: gains depend strongly on environment, worker budget and traffic. Five short repetitions with uncontrolled host activity are exploratory evidence, not production forecasts.

The previous native-loop advantage does not reproduce in the large macOS full-actor case, while Linux sharding remains promising here. These experiments do not isolate which envelope, allocation, wakeup, placement or reactor cost explains the difference; profiling is needed for causal attribution.

Native Linux reproduction on fede

The November 6 reproduction adds 525 successful measured processes on an AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D. It uses the same clean measured revision and seven variants, with five repetitions per cell. The complete job, including producers, observers and TCP server threads, shares CPUs 2–5 (four physical cores in one L3 group), at nice=10. Workers are not pinned individually and the host is shared. This is a separate environment from the ARM64 VM, not a controlled kernel or CPU comparison.

At 1,024 actors, fixed-16 sharding is 16.5% faster with 85.3% lower completion p99 at four workers. At two workers it is 3.8% slower with 19.8% lower p99. The larger VM throughput gain is therefore not a portable constant. Four workers also do not universally beat two within this four-core job budget; the producer/observer threads compete for those CPUs too, and profiling is needed to explain the tails.

The other cells prevent a simple winner claim. At four workers and 128 actors, fixed-16 sharding has a 2.305M/s median versus Tokio's 1.878M/s, but p99 rises from 0.156 to 0.555 ms; the throughput run ranges overlap. At two workers under skew, cold p99 improves (0.237 to 0.116 ms) while overall p99 worsens (0.482 to 0.893 ms) and throughput falls. Native Linux reproduces the scheduling tradeoffs, not a universal fairness win.

For persistent TCP at four workers, medians are 588k/s and 0.821 ms for fixed-16 sharding versus 513k/s and 2.548 ms for Tokio. At two workers throughput is similar and sharded p99 is worse (2.005 versus 1.339 ms). Timer throughput is close across the reference and fixed-16 paths, about 59–61k/s. Deliberately blocking handlers show similar throughput but lower sharded tails; they remain non-preemptible. The TCP server and producer setup remain common controls, not an optimized client.

Throughput and overall p99 do not establish fairness

In Linux's four-worker hotspot case, fixed-16 sharding improves overall p99 from 1.465 to 1.053 ms, but cold-actor p99 worsens from 0.553 to 1.305 ms. Static placement can isolate some traffic and concentrate other traffic. Use cold/hot breakdowns, not only the overall distribution, when deciding a scheduling policy.

Batches are not a universal improvement on existing Tokio. With two macOS workers and 128 actors, Tokio-adaptive reaches 492k/s versus baseline 392k/s, but their run ranges overlap (453–548k and 300–509k). With four workers, the same case is roughly 596k versus 602k/s. At 1,024 actors, Linux Tokio-adaptive trails its unmodified Tokio baseline at both budgets. Fixed batch 16 can improve on forced yield-every-message without improving on Tokio's existing cooperative policy; always keep async as the reference, not just the artificially frequent-yield control.

The balanced RPC cases usually have at most one outstanding request per actor, so they often do not sustain a mailbox backlog. Differences between those cells cannot automatically be credited to batch size. The hotspot case exercises a busy mailbox; burst and offered-rate sweeps should quantify turn policy further. Also, -1 means an explicit one-message turn, not the absence of a batching policy.

Async waits, networking and blocking work

Persistent TCP on macOS clusters around 150k echoes/s across these designs, with wide overlapping ranges. Linux with two workers fixed-16 sharding reaches 349k/s versus 274k/s for Tokio; Linux with four workers reaches 377k versus 302k/s, with mixed latency outcomes (fixed sharding p99 2.050 ms versus Tokio 2.002 ms at four workers). The common server has one native thread per socket; this is not a complete optimized application/network stack.

The 1 ms async-timer case also changes by environment and worker count. It measures runtime/OS timer behavior plus scheduling, not calibrated 1 ms service or CPU work.

The blocking case deliberately sleeps inside an async handler. Its requested 100 µs sleep has Linux with two workers handler p99 around 3.7 ms. Sharding can reduce completion p99 while also reducing throughput; Linux with four workers fixed-16 is about 1,403/s versus Tokio's 1,736/s, with p99 about216 versus310 ms. This is a scheduling tradeoff under blocking misuse, not preemption, faster CPU execution, or proof of a better blocking backend.

Correctness and useful library changes

The experiment reuses actual Spawned lifecycle machinery instead of shipping the native benchmark loop. Review caught and corrected idle-time turn accounting, stop during a yield, and last-actor runtime teardown under detached helpers, blocking children and monitor waiters. The process-owned pool now has explicit terminal shutdown after actors/helpers complete; documented current-thread and caller-context limitations remain.

Agy also found a general completion-status bug: a dropped completion sender could make an async wait return Kill while synchronous exit_reason() still returned None and ChildHandle::is_alive() returned true. The separate fix preserves a published final reason, treats closed-without-reason as Kill, and allows the already-exited blocking fast path to work without entering another runtime. Tests cover both tasks and thread completion modes and resource-exhaustion startup.

The performance dataset is pinned to clean revision 9b22346, before both the getter-only status fix and the later shutdown-publication fix. The latter closes/drains/discards admitted requests before reporting ordinary actor completion; its deterministic regression fails on the historical source and passes with the fix. Fede functional checks use corrected source separately. All successful benchmark cells are of that source/binary; performance was not remeasured after the status-path fix. The later fix has separate validation. Do not describe these numbers as measurements of an unrecorded final-branch binary.

What to do next

  1. Keep the merged completion-status and shutdown-publication fixes covered by regressions, document blocking-pool / dedicated-reactor capacity, and retain the runtime experiment as opt-in research.
  2. Profile the representative macOS loss and Linux gain, then test actor-to-actor chains/fan-out with controlled same/cross-shard placement and skew. This decides whether locality or a specific wakeup cost justifies a new supported backend.
  3. Run fixed-arrival-rate saturation tests with intended-arrival timestamps, producer-lag accounting, cold tails and queue/RSS time series. Closed-loop RPC does not establish latency targets under overload.
  4. Separately evaluate borrowing blocking workers per active handler to address persistent blocking actors exhausting the finite pool. That design is proposed, not implemented; sequencing, migration/TLS, async work and shutdown need review.

Research protocol and decision criteria describe these follow-ups. Add another kernel backend, affinity policy or custom work-stealing executor only after the evidence identifies the bottleneck or missing behavior.

Reading the figures

Bars show medians; whiskers show observed min/max across fresh processes, not confidence intervals. p99 is the median of run-level handler-completion p99s, not a pooled quantile. Caller-observed latency is retained separately in the CSV. Closed-loop traffic has at most one request per producer; these are not fixed-arrival-rate SLO tests. Compare within a platform and worker budget; The linux2/linux4 studies use a four-vCPU OrbStack VM/container; fede2/fede4 use native x86-64 Linux on a shared server with the entire process tree restricted to four physical CPUs. These are separate environments, not an isolated OS/kernel comparison.

Compatibility and interpretation

The sharded backend is Tokio-based and statically places actors; it adds neither work stealing nor CPU affinity. Current-thread runtime restrictions apply, including unsupported block_in_place. The process pool and its explicit terminal shutdown are experimental. External Context helper calls retain their caller-runtime binding. Full actor tests do not make those runtime differences disappear.

The initial actor-count-owned pool was rejected after agy review found premature helper/child runtime teardown. The corrected pool has explicit lifetime, and turn-budget/cancellation regressions accompany it. Keep default Tokio until both workload evidence and lifecycle ownership justify a supported alternative.
